why: The error codes a host exposes are the last vocabulary crossing the engine boundary
with nothing behind it. Every other shared name in this repository is generated or
gated: field types, function aliases, the runtime projection, the runtime versions,
the shared bounds, the structural rules, the event kinds, even the preset facade's
method list. Error codes were not.
What the boundary actually carries is `@errorName(err)` -- see `runtimeError` in
packages/zig/wasm/src/abi.zig -- so a host code that names an engine error is
coupled to the spelling of a Zig error, and nothing said so. Rename the error and
the host keeps matching a string the engine no longer produces: no compile error, no
test failure, just a code that stops arriving. `scene-safe.ts` then falls through to
a plain Error and the caller loses the code it was switching on.
So every code in the gated host unions is classified here.
shared    -- the host code is an engine error name, spelled identically.
renamed   -- the host deliberately re-words an engine error. The mapping has to
exist in scene-safe.ts, and this file is where the pair is recorded.
hostOnly  -- the host raises it itself; the engine has no such error.
vestigial -- nothing can currently raise it. Kept in the exported union, recorded
here so it is a decision rather than a leftover.
A code in none of the four fails the gate, and so does a `shared` or `renamed` code
whose engine error no longer exists.
Found on the first run: six codes in the vestigial list below. They date from when
TypeScript executed scenes itself; the engine took that over and the vocabulary was
never trimmed. They are exported types no code path can produce, which is what this
gate exists to stop happening again.
Found on the second: the unions were only half the surface. A host also names an
engine error by comparing a bare string literal against one, and those live wherever
the comparison is -- not in errors.ts, and not necessarily in this package.
packages/ts/runtime had ten of them and no gate had ever looked at it. executeGraph.ts
reconstructs a cycle, an empty pipe and a missing value from GraphCycle, EmptyPipe and
MissingValue; zig-preset.ts translates six more into the messages the TypeScript
executor used to produce. Rename any of them in Zig and the comparison stops matching:
executeGraph downgrades a cycle to a generic execution error, and callZigPreset
surfaces the raw code in place of its message. No compile error, no failing test --
the same silence the unions were gated to end.
So `matchSources` names the trees to scan and `matched` classifies every literal found
there that the engine also raises. A code already classified above needs no second
entry: `shared` and `renamed` each assert the engine error still exists, which is the
pin a match site needs. `matched` carries the rest, and is checked in both directions
-- the engine must still raise it, and a scanned source must still compare against it
-- so neither a rename in Zig nor a deleted call site can leave the list stale.
